# Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review of Sacubitril/Valsartan

## Introduction
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge with high morbidity and mortality. Historically, pharmacotherapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) focused on blocking the overactive renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. However, the discovery of the natriuretic peptide system, which promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and reverses adverse remodeling, suggested a dual-pathway approach. Sacubitril/valsartan is a first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) that simultaneously blocks the angiotensin II type 1 ($AT_1$) receptor and inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme responsible for degrading natriuretic peptides [1]. This review summarizes the clinical evidence, physiological impact, and therapeutic role of sacubitril/valsartan across the heart failure spectrum.

## The Evolution of ARNI Therapy
Prior attempts at dual inhibition of the RAAS and neutral endopeptidase (neprilysin) focused on omapatrilat, which inhibited both neprilysin and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). However, omapatrilat was associated with unacceptable rates of life-threatening angioedema due to a double-inhibition of bradykinin breakdown [2]. Sacubitril/valsartan avoided this safety concern by combining a neprilysin inhibitor prodrug (sacubitril) with an angiotensin receptor blocker (valsartan), maintaining therapeutic efficacy without the disproportionate risk of angioedema [1]. Early clinical studies confirmed its potent blood pressure-lowering effect in systemic hypertension [3].

## Clinical Evidence in Chronic HFrEF
The clinical development of sacubitril/valsartan in chronic HFrEF was defined by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [1]. In this double-blind trial, 8,442 patients with chronic HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%) were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan (97/103 mg twice daily) or enalapril (10 mg twice daily). The trial was stopped early due to an overwhelming benefit in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, which was reduced by 20% in the ARNI group. Sacubitril/valsartan also showed significant reductions in all-cause mortality, clinical progression of heart failure [4], and sudden cardiac death [5] compared with enalapril. Subsequent analyses showed that even lower-than-target doses of sacubitril/valsartan retained superiority over enalapril, confirming its efficacy across various clinical subpopulations [6].

## Acute Decompensated Heart Failure and In-Hospital Initiation
While PARADIGM-HF established ARNI efficacy in stable chronic outpatients, the PIONEER-HF trial evaluated its role in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) [7]. Hospitalized HFrEF patients stabilized after an ADHF episode were randomized to in-hospital initiation of either sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril. ARNI therapy led to a significantly greater reduction in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and a reduction in serious clinical events, such as rehospitalization [8]. The TRANSITION and TITRATION trials supported these findings, demonstrating that in-hospital or early post-discharge initiation of sacubitril/valsartan is both feasible and safe [9,10].

## Mechanisms of Benefit: Reverse Remodeling and Biomarkers
The clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan are closely linked to reverse cardiac remodeling. The PROVE-HF trial demonstrated that the initiation of sacubitril/valsartan led to rapid reductions in NT-proBNP, which strongly correlated with improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end-diastolic volume index, and left atrial volume index [11]. Similarly, the EVALUATE-HF trial examined vascular stiffness, finding significant improvements in central aortic pressures and cardiac structure [12].

## Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF) and the EF Continuum
The therapeutic utility of sacubitril/valsartan has also been extensively explored in patients with higher ejection fractions. Following the phase II PARAMOUNT trial, which showed reductions in NT-proBNP and left atrial size in HFpEF patients (LVEF ≥45%) [13], the phase III PARAGON-HF trial was launched [14]. PARAGON-HF compared sacubitril/valsartan to valsartan alone in 4,822 patients with LVEF ≥45% [15]. Although the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint (a 13% relative risk reduction in total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death; p=0.059), subgroup analyses suggested heterogeneity of treatment effect. Specifically, patients with lower LVEF (45–57%) and women derived significant clinical benefit [15].

A subsequent pooled analysis of both PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated that the benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend up to a LVEF of approximately 55-60%, confirming its role in heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF) [16]. However, the PARALLAX trial showed that while sacubitril/valsartan reduced NT-proBNP in HFpEF, it did not significantly improve 6-minute walk distance compared to individualized comparator therapies [17].

## Other Settings: Post-Myocardial Infarction and Advanced HF
The PARADISE-MI trial evaluated sacubitril/valsartan in patients with acute myocardial infarction complicated by reduced LVEF or pulmonary congestion, but it failed to show a significant reduction in cardiovascular death or incident HF compared to ramipril [18]. In advanced HFrEF, the LIFE trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly lower NT-proBNP levels or improve clinical outcomes compared to valsartan in patients with NYHA class IV symptoms [19].

## Guidelines, Tolerability, and Clinical Management
Reflecting this vast clinical trial database, the 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines and 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guidelines recommend sacubitril/valsartan as a Class I (or first-line) therapy for patients with HFrEF [20,21]. Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) including ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), and SGLT2 inhibitors has been projected to dramatically increase lifetime survival [22].

Regarding safety, sacubitril/valsartan is generally well-tolerated. Symptomatic hypotension is more common with ARNI than with ACE inhibitors, but it rarely leads to treatment discontinuation [1,7,10]. Importantly, sacubitril/valsartan is associated with lower rates of hyperkalemia [23] and a slower decline in renal function compared to enalapril, even in patients with chronic kidney disease [24,25,26,27]. It also reduces the incidence of new-onset diabetes [28]. Clinical management requires a 36-hour washout period when switching from an ACE inhibitor to prevent angioedema [20,21]. Treatment benefit has been shown to persist across different age groups [29] and independent of recent hospitalization status in HFpEF [30].

## Conclusion
Sacubitril/valsartan represents a major breakthrough in heart failure therapeutics. Its dual mechanism of action offers unmatched clinical efficacy in HFrEF, stabilizes patients during acute decompensation, and benefits patients across a broad continuum of ejection fractions, particularly those with HFmrEF.
